item.description:

👤 Divyansh Chawla, Khushi Agarwal, Isshaan Singh
Industrial robotic systems rely on predictive maintenance to prevent failures and optimize operational efficiency. However, accurately detecting faults such as protective stop and grip loss remains challenging due to high-dimensional sensor data and inherent noise. To address this, we propose a quantum multi-output network combined with cycle-consistent autoencoders, leveraging quantum feature encoding to enhance fault detection. The model effectively reduces dimensionality while mitigating quantum noise propagation, ensuring computational efficiency with fewer qubits. This paper studies how much Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) work can be avoided while preserving optimization quality in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). Six QPUminimization strategies are evaluated: preprocessing, pretraining, surrogate modeling, adaptive stopping, adaptive shots, and measurement reuse. The accurate computational solution of the time-harmonic Maxwell equations remains a central challenge in computational electromagnetics due to the indefinite nature of the double curl operator, the presence of spurious modes, and the high computational cost of resolving oscillatory solutions at large frequencies. In this work, we develop a hp-finite element method to solve the double-curl operator of time-harmonic Maxwell equations, as well as the resulting oscillatory modes. The approach uses Engquist-Majda absorbing boundary conditions and adaptive hp-refinements to efficiently handle unbounded domains and complex field behavior. item.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materials, with potential implications for future spintronic technologies.

The lateral photovoltaic effect (LPE) in a SiO2/TeO2/Bi2Te3/n-Si hybrid heterostructure was investigated as a function of light wavelength, temperature, illumination position, and magnetic field. The Schottky barrier height of the structure was estimated to be ΦB = 0.3 eV using the thermionic emission model. This indicates the transition between two dominant photovoltaic channels associated with carrier photogeneration in the Si substrate and Bi2Te3 film. The Si-related contribution was found to be sensitive to the magnetic field, whereas the Bi2Te3-related contribution remains nearly unaffected. item.title: Magnetic sculpting transforms single-source fields into predetermined shapes with mathematical precision
item.description:
📚 Physics News
Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties. Today, creating such tailored magnetic fields requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application—a complex and resource-intensive process.

Spatial textures of magnetic order, such as domain walls and skyrmions, are fundamental objects in magnetism. In rhombohedral multilayer graphene, magnetic order involves spin and valley degrees of freedom, opening the possibility of qualitatively new spatial textures. Here, we explore this possibility through a microscopic study of a one-dimensional domain wall in the valley-imbalanced quarter-metal phase of rhombohedral graphene. We uncover two different classes of domain walls. Quantum supervised learning (QSL) is increasingly investigated for intrusion detection, yet its behavior under adversarial manipulation remains insufficiently characterized in network-security settings. item.description:

👤 Jeong Youn-Chang, Kim Seok, Hong Changho, Ji Se-Wan
Quantum digital signature (QDS) provides information-theoretic security and enables fundamental cryptographic functionalities, including integrity, non-repudiation, and data origin authentication. Existing QDS implementations, however, assign fixed user roles - signer, authenticator, and verifier - which limits their applicability in practical quantum networks, where role flexibility is essential. In this work, we implement a QDS protocol on a three-user fiber-optic quantum network in which any participant can dynamically assume the role of signer. Every node uses an identical design for encoding and decoding time-bin quantum states, enabling flexible signer assignment without hardware reconfiguration.
